_about: CERTIFICATION SENSITIVITY FLAGS — the rules src/lib/cbfc.js reads the script against. Content, so it lives here (rule 2 in CLAUDE.md). Nothing in this file is legal advice and the page says so wherever it shows any of it.

HOW A RULE IS WRITTEN. `kind` is 'requirement' (a statutory or regulator's step the producer has to take — a disclaimer, a permission, a certificate), 'review' (content the Board's examining committee weighs under the certification guidelines) or 'caution' (a legal risk outside certification — defamation, trade marks). `reads` names what the rule is tested against: 'dialogue', 'action', 'heading', 'paren', 'synopsis' (the scene row's own line) and 'elements' (the breakdown's tags). Smoking, animals and uniforms are about what is ON SCREEN, so they do not read dialogue: a line that calls somebody a dog is not a dog on set.

TERMS. Every tier carries `en` and `ta` lists. `ta` is ROMANISED Tamil / Tanglish, the way this app's sample script and most Tamil units write dialogue; `taScript` is a short Tamil-script list. They are STARTER LISTS: incomplete by design, and the page says so. Matching is whole-word and case-blind; a trailing `*` means 'and any ending' (stab* finds stabs, stabbed, stabbing; kolai* finds kolaikaaran), which is also how Tamil's suffixes are reached. A term with a space is a phrase.

THE RATING HINT is the app's own heuristic, not the Board's criteria. Each tier names the lowest category the app GUESSES that content tends to land in (`hint`), or null where the content does not by itself move the category (tobacco has not affected the category since the 2012 COTPA amendment). The film-level hint is the highest tier that fired. The categories are the ones in force after the Cinematograph (Amendment) Act, 2023 and the Cinematograph (Certification) Rules, 2024 — the same list deliverables.json uses.

SOURCES AND HONESTY. Every rule cites `source` (what the requirement rests on), `sourceUrls` (where it was read) and `checked` (when). `confidence` says how well it is known ('official' — read on the regulator's own site; 'secondary' — law-firm or press reports of the official text, consistent with each other; 'uncertain' — reported, not confirmed), and `uncertain` says what in particular to check. If a rule changes, change it here and move `checked`. THE SOURCE CHECK OF 8 OCTOBER 2026 re-read these in a real browser, which earlier passes could not: 16 of the 18 cited URLs answer, cbfcindia.gov.in and awbi.gov.in and mib.gov.in among them. Nothing was found to be WRONG. What changed is precision — the 1991 notification is numbered S.O. 836(E), the 2026 revision is dated 16 September and SUPERSEDES rather than amends it, the anti-drug wording is confirmed verbatim, and rule 2C's notification number and date are confirmed. Two things are worth knowing before anyone re-checks. The 2026 guidelines text is still not published by CBFC or MIB, so every clause NUMBER quoted below is the 1991 one and none has been checked against the current text — CBFC's own clarification that the core provisions are unchanged is why they are still quoted at all. And cbfcindia.gov.in's certification page is STALER than the law: it still describes UA as 'below the age of twelve', three years after the 2024 Rules split it. An official site is not automatically the most current source, which is the opposite of the assumption this note used to make.
A rule `id` is not a storage key (the page stores nothing), so it may be renamed — but the tests name them.
disclaimer: These flags are a word search over your script, not a reading of the film. They miss things a person would see and flag things that are fine. The likely-rating line is this app's guess, not the Board's criteria and not legal advice — the Board judges the finished film as a whole. Check anything that matters with your regional CBFC office or a lawyer.

ratings.label: UA 7+
ratings.means: Unrestricted, with parental guidance for children under 7.

ratings.label: UA 13+
ratings.means: Unrestricted, with parental guidance for children under 13.

ratings.label: UA 16+
ratings.means: Unrestricted, with parental guidance for children under 16.

ratingsSource.source: Cinematograph (Amendment) Act, 2023 and the Cinematograph (Certification) Rules, 2024 — notified 15 March 2024, replacing the 1983 Rules — which split UA into UA 7+, UA 13+ and UA 16+ and moved applications to the e-Cinepramaan portal. The markers reached the certification GUIDELINES later, by an amendment in May 2025, which is why a 1991-dated guideline document can still be current and yet name them.
ratingsSource._note: TWO TRAPS for whoever re-checks this. The CBFC's own certification page still describes UA as 'below the age of twelve' and has not been updated for the 2024 split, so the official site is STALER than the Rules — do not 'correct' the three markers back to UA 12 from it. And the Act also provides an S certificate, 'restricted to specialized audiences such as doctors or scientists'; it is deliberately absent from the list above, because that list is an ORDERED SEVERITY SCALE the rating hint walks and scripts/test-delivery.mjs asserts exactly, and S is orthogonal to severity rather than above A.

guidelinesNote.text: The Board's certification guidelines under section 5B(2) of the Cinematograph Act, 1952 were revised on 16 SEPTEMBER 2026. The operative words, as CBFC itself published them, are 'in exercise of powers conferred by sub-section (2) of section 5B of the Cinematograph Act, 1952 (37 of 1952) and in supersession of notification No. S.O. 836(E), dated the 6th December, 1991' — so the 1991 guidelines are SUPERSEDED, not amended. CBFC's clarification of 19 September 2026, issued through PIB and reposted by the Board, says only two substantive changes have been made in 35 years: the UA age markers (2024, written into the guidelines in May 2025) and this anti-drug message, and that 'except for these two changes, the core provisions and principles governing film certification have remained unchanged'. The clauses quoted below are therefore the 1991 ones, which the Board says still hold in substance. The 2026 text itself is still not published on cbfcindia.gov.in or mib.gov.in, so no clause NUMBER below has been checked against it.

rules.label: Smoking or tobacco on screen
rules.what: Any film that shows tobacco products or their use has to carry the anti-tobacco material the COTPA film rules prescribe, and give the Board an editorial justification for the display.
do: Anti-tobacco health spots of at least 30 seconds at the beginning and the middle of the film.

An audio-visual disclaimer on the ill effects of tobacco, at least 20 seconds each, at the beginning and the middle. SETTLED 8 October 2026: rule 8 says 'beginning and middle of the film' and never mentions the interval.
A prominent static health warning at the bottom of the screen for as long as the tobacco is on screen.
A strong editorial justification for the display, given to the Board with the application — rule 8 is a CONDITION OF CERTIFICATION, so the Board does not certify the film until these are met.

The static warning is black on white and in the language of the film (or of the dub or subtitle): 'Smoking causes cancer' or 'Smoking kills' for smoking forms, 'Tobacco causes cancer' or 'Tobacco kills' for smokeless ones (rule 8(4)).

NO BRAND. Rules 9 and 10 bar brand display, product placement and close-ups of packs, and require brand names and logos to be cropped or masked — dress the prop, not just the warning. Rule 11(5) says the same for online content.

Streaming: rule 11 requires the same 30-second spots, static message and 20-second disclaimer of the PUBLISHER of online curated content — the platform, not you. The start date is not written in the Gazette: rule 1(2) says three months after publication, and publication was 31 May 2023, so 1 September 2023 is COMPUTED rather than stated. The spots and the disclaimer are supplied on mohfw.gov.in / ntcp.mohfw.gov.in.
rules.source: COTPA Rules, 2004 — RULES 7 TO 10, inserted by G.S.R. 786(E) (27 October 2011, in force 14 November 2011); rules 7 and 8 substituted by G.S.R. 708(E) (21 September 2012, in force 2 October 2012). Rule 8 governs films CBFC-certified after 2 October 2012; rule 7 covers older ones. Rule 11, inserted by G.S.R. 400(E) (31 May 2023), puts the same material on ONLINE CURATED CONTENT — and the duty there is the PUBLISHER's, meaning the platform, not the producer. DO NOT CITE RULE 4(6): this entry used to, and it is dead law. Rule 4(6) was the flat ban on tobacco in cinema and television, and the Delhi High Court QUASHED it in Mahesh Bhatt v Union of India, WP(C) 18761/2005, as ultra vires section 31 and violative of Article 19(1)(a). Read in the Gazette PDFs on ntcp.mohfw.gov.in, 8 October 2026.
rules.uncertain: Both old doubts are SETTLED against the Gazette: 'middle' means the middle of the film, and the final rule 11 carries no non-skippable language, so that draft was not carried through. What is left is small. The 1 September 2023 start is computed from rule 1(2), not printed. And on the quashing of rule 4(6) the sources disagree about the date — one opinion in the judgment PDF is signed 7 February 2008 while tobaccocontrollaws.org dates the decision 23 January 2009 — and the final bench outcome was not confirmed. What is certain is that rule 4(6) is not the provision to cite.

rules.label: Narcotic drugs or psychotropic substances
rules.what: The September 2026 guidelines require scenes depicting, involving the use, consumption or trafficking of narcotic drugs or psychotropic substances to carry a disclaimer or statutory warning, and the guidelines bar scenes that encourage, justify or glamorise drug addiction.
do: Carry the on-screen message fixed by the guidelines: "Illicit Narcotics Destroy Health and Guarantees Imprisonment. Say No to Drugs." — wording CONFIRMED 8 October 2026 against CBFC's own published clause and three independent reports, including the lower-case 'to'.
Make sure the scene does not encourage, justify or glamorise drug use.
rules.source: Guidelines for certification of films under section 5B(2), Cinematograph Act, 1952, as revised by the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting and notified on 16 SEPTEMBER 2026 (the date is CBFC's own, not a press inference). SEPARATELY, for a release that streams: an MIB advisory dated 24 August 2026 asks OTT platforms to display the SAME warning during scenes of drug consumption or use, continuing an advisory of 26 November 2024; private TV channels were told the same. Those are ADVISORIES, not rules, and MediaNama reported it could not find the August one on MIB's own site — treat them as a strong expectation rather than a citable obligation.
rules.uncertain: Settled 8 October 2026: the date is 16 September 2026 and the wording is confirmed verbatim. What is still unread is the notification text itself, which is not published — so the warning's required SIZE, PLACEMENT and DURATION on screen are unknown, and the OTT advisory is reported rather than sighted at source.

rules.label: Alcohol
rules.what: The guidelines ask that scenes tending to justify or glorify drinking are not shown. Drinking itself is not barred and needs no disclaimer under the guidelines as reported; how the scene treats it is what the committee weighs.
do: Check the scene does not justify or glorify drinking.
A liquor brand visible in frame is also a trade-mark and surrogate-advertising question — see 'Real people, brands and institutions'.
rules.source: Guidelines for certification of films, notified 6 December 1991 as S.O. 836(E), and SUPERSEDED on 16 September 2026 by revised guidelines under section 5B(2). CBFC's own clarification (PIB, 19 September 2026) says the core provisions and principles are unchanged across the two changes made in 35 years, so this clause survives in substance; the 2026 text is not published, so its clause NUMBER here is the 1991 one and is unverified.
rules.uncertain: Many Tamil releases carry a 'drinking is injurious to health' caption; that is common practice, and we did not find it stated as a requirement. Ask the regional office.

rules.label: Animals on screen
rules.what: An owner hiring out or lending a performing animal for a film must give the Animal Welfare Board of India prior information and a fitness certificate, and AWBI now gives its no-objection certificate only after a pre-shoot permission. The guidelines separately ask that cruelty to or abuse of animals is not presented needlessly.
do: The producer applies to AWBI online for pre-shoot permission BEFORE the shoot day, with the animal owner's details, with the pre-shoot fitness certificate (and vaccination records for dogs and cats).

THE BULL BAN IS THE ONE TO CHECK FIRST on a Tamil shoot: G.S.R. 528(E) bars bears, monkeys, tigers, panthers, lions and BULLS from being exhibited or trained as performing animals. A bull in shot is not a permission question, it is a prohibition question, and the answer may be that the scene cannot be filmed with a real animal at all. We have not checked what later litigation has done to the bull entry.

The animal's OWNER must be registered with AWBI — the manual gives Rs 5,000 once every five years, with inspection — and rule 7's prior information is the owner's duty, not yours. Check the registration before you book the animal.
Have a veterinary doctor at the shooting spot: that is what AWBI's manual asks for. It does not ask for an 'animal welfare officer', despite what is often said.
After the shoot, file the self-declaration that no cruelty was inflicted (and the transport declaration with photographs), and obtain the AWBI certificate for the film.

Background scenes, computer-graphics animals, stock shots and foreign shoots are the ONLY cases in which AWBI will consider a direct post-shoot NOC with no pre-shoot permission. They are not exempt from AWBI paperwork — the direct NOC is the dearer of the two — so say which applies and budget for it. AWBI also takes applications only from the producer or production company, or someone it authorises in writing: it says it has no agents.
rules.source: Performing Animals (Registration) Rules, 2001 — notification S.O. 267(E), 26 March 2001, under the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act, 1960; amended once, by S.O. 35(E) of 8 January 2002, which does not touch rule 7. Rule 7, 'Prior information for use of performing animals in films', read from the Gazette text on 8 October 2026: it carries NO notice period and no 'thirty days' — the only thirty days in the Rules is rule 3(1), the one-time registration window of 2001 — and the duty under it falls on the ANIMAL'S OWNER, not the producer. Separately: G.S.R. 528(E) of 11 July 2011 (MoEF), superseding G.S.R. 619(E) of 14 October 1998, BANS the exhibition or training as performing animals of bears, monkeys, tigers, panthers, lions and BULLS. Plus AWBI's own performing-animal procedure, and the certification guidelines on cruelty to animals.
rules.uncertain: That the Board asks for the AWBI certificate before it certifies is widely stated and is common practice; we did not find it written as a rule in an official text. On the fees, a correction: AWBI's page gives ₹25,000 for pre-shoot permission and ₹30,000 for a direct post-shoot NOC, and the 'revised fee structure' wording on that page attaches to the OTHER categories (race horses, events, circuses, polo ponies, elephants), not to these two — so the earlier note implying both were under revision was wrong. The page carries no date, so confirm before paying. Unchecked: what later litigation has done to the bull entry in G.S.R. 528(E).

rules.label: Violence and gore
rules.what: The guidelines ask that scenes glorifying or justifying violence are not shown, and that violence is not dwelt on beyond what the story needs. How much and how it is shown is what moves a film between categories.
do: Decide what the camera holds on. The committee reads the cut, not the page; the same scene can pass or be cut depending on duration and detail.
Keep a clean alternative take of the most graphic moments — a requested cut is quicker to make from coverage than by trimming frames.
rules.source: Guidelines for certification of films, notified 6 December 1991 as S.O. 836(E), and SUPERSEDED on 16 September 2026 by revised guidelines under section 5B(2). CBFC's own clarification (PIB, 19 September 2026) says the core provisions and principles are unchanged across the two changes made in 35 years, so this clause survives in substance; the 2026 text is not published, so its clause NUMBER here is the 1991 one and is unverified.

rules.label: Sexual content
rules.what: The guidelines ask that human sensibilities are not offended by vulgarity, obscenity or depravity, that women are not degraded or denigrated, and that sexual violence — attempted rape, rape or any form of molestation — is avoided, and where the theme needs it, kept to the minimum with no detail shown.
do: For sexual violence, the guideline asks for the minimum and no detail: plan the coverage so the scene can be told without it.
Nudity or explicit sexual content usually means an A certificate; decide early whether the release plan can carry one.
rules.source: Guidelines for certification of films, notified 6 December 1991 as S.O. 836(E), and SUPERSEDED on 16 September 2026 by revised guidelines under section 5B(2). CBFC's own clarification (PIB, 19 September 2026) says the core provisions and principles are unchanged across the two changes made in 35 years, so this clause survives in substance; the 2026 text is not published, so its clause NUMBER here is the 1991 one and is unverified.

rules.label: Abusive language and slurs
rules.what: The guidelines ask that dual-meaning words that obviously cater to baser instincts are not allowed and that human sensibilities are not offended by vulgarity. Examining committees routinely mute specific words; each muted word is a sound edit and, after certification, a re-certification.
do: Record a clean alternative line (wild track or in the dub) for every flagged word you want to keep the option of losing.
Subtitles count: a word muted in the mix but left in the English subtitle is still on screen.
rules.source: Guidelines for certification of films, notified 6 December 1991 as S.O. 836(E), and SUPERSEDED on 16 September 2026 by revised guidelines under section 5B(2). CBFC's own clarification (PIB, 19 September 2026) says the core provisions and principles are unchanged across the two changes made in 35 years, so this clause survives in substance; the 2026 text is not published, so its clause NUMBER here is the 1991 one and is unverified.
rules.uncertain: Press reports of the 2026 revision did not describe its wording on language; the 1991 clauses are assumed retained.

rules.label: Caste, religion or community references
rules.what: The guidelines ask that visuals or words contemptuous of racial, religious or other groups are not presented, and that communal, obscurantist, anti-scientific or anti-national attitudes are not promoted. A reference is not a problem; contempt is. These terms are flagged so a person reads the scene with that question in mind — in Tamil cinema caste depictions are also where protests and court petitions after release most often start.
do: Read every flagged line for who is speaking and whether the film endorses it.
Where a real community is named, consider whether the scene needs the name.
rules.source: Guidelines for certification of films, 6 December 1991 (S.O. 836(E)), clause (xii) as reported — SUPERSEDED on 16 September 2026 but unchanged in substance per CBFC's clarification. The clause NUMBER is from the 1991 text and could not be checked against the 2026 notification, which is not published.

rules.label: Real people, brands and institutions
rules.what: Defamation is one of the grounds in section 5B(1) of the Cinematograph Act on which a certificate can be refused, and a real person, party or company shown in a bad light is a civil and criminal defamation risk long after certification. A brand visible or named on screen is a trade-mark question and, for a sponsor, a contract one.
do: For a real person: consent in writing, or change the name and the identifying details.
For a brand: a release from the owner, a placement contract, or a fictional label — art department, not post.
A disclaimer that the story is fictional helps but does not cure a portrayal anyone can identify.
rules.source: Cinematograph Act, 1952, section 5B(1) (defamation as a ground); the law of defamation and the Trade Marks Act, 1999 apply independently of certification.
rules.uncertain: A word list cannot recognise a real person's name. Named institutions are found by a capitalised name before a word like Hospital or College; read the flagged lines, and look for real names the list cannot know.

rules.label: National emblem, flag, police or armed-forces uniforms
rules.what: The guidelines ask that national symbols and emblems are not shown except as the Emblems and Names (Prevention of Improper Use) Act, 1950 allows. The State Emblem of India (Prohibition of Improper Use) Act, 2005, the Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act, 1971 (the flag and the anthem) and the Flag Code of India, 2002 govern how the emblem, the flag and the anthem may be used. Police and armed-forces uniforms on actors are costume; shooting in them in public is a permission question.
do: Show the flag and the anthem only in ways those Acts allow — no flag as a costume, a cloth or a prop that is handled carelessly.
Use a fictional insignia rather than the State Emblem on props such as a police cap badge or a letterhead, unless you have checked the use is permitted.
For a public location shot in police or forces uniform, take the jurisdictional police's permission — the location permission usually covers it, but say so in the application.

Films about the armed forces: get the Ministry of Defence NOC question answered BEFORE you shoot, not at submission. In 2020 MoD wrote to CBFC asking that production houses be advised to obtain an NOC for any film, documentary or web series on an Army theme, and reporting since describes scripts being run past military officials before production. It is an advisory to the Board rather than a statute — but it has teeth: a Minister of State for Defence told Parliament in February 2022 that an NOC had been REFUSED for a film, on national-security and image grounds. MoD weighs national security, law and order, discipline in the forces, service ethos and the forces' image. Budget for the delay.
rules.source: Guidelines for certification of films, 6 December 1991 (S.O. 836(E)), clause (xix) as reported — SUPERSEDED on 16 September 2026 but unchanged in substance per CBFC's clarification; the clause NUMBER is unverified against the 2026 text. Emblems and Names (Prevention of Improper Use) Act, 1950; State Emblem of India (Prohibition of Improper Use) Act, 2005; Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act, 1971; Flag Code of India, 2002.
rules.uncertain: The guideline clause is reported consistently, but its NUMBER is unverified against the unpublished 2026 text. The police-permission point is still common practice rather than a rule we can cite. The MoD NOC is confirmed to be live and to have been refused at least once, but we have found no notification or circular text — only reporting and a parliamentary answer, so its exact scope (Army only, or all three services; feature films only, or web series too) is not settled. A uniform worn by an actor on a closed set is costume: the Official Secrets Act provisions on military uniform are about DECEPTION, which a film set is not.

rules.label: Children on set, and in hazardous scenes

tiers.label: a child (under 14, or named as a child)
aged 14 to 17, by the age the script gives
a hazard in the same scene

rules.what: Under the Child and Adolescent Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act and its 2017 rules, a child under 14 may take part in an audio-visual production only with the District Magistrate's permission and on the rule's conditions. The guidelines separately bar scenes showing children as victims or perpetrators of violence, forcing children to witness violence, or subjecting them to any form of abuse.
do: Before the shoot, take the permission of the District Magistrate for the district where you are shooting, for every child artist. Rule 2C names what you file: an undertaking in FORM C, the list of child participants, and the consent of each parent or guardian — all BEFORE the activity starts. No child may be made to take part against their own will and consent, whatever the parent has signed.
No more than five hours of work a day and no more than three hours without rest; one responsible person on set for every five children at most.

No child to work more than TWENTY-SEVEN CONSECUTIVE DAYS, and education arranged so school lessons are not interrupted. This was stated here as 'no child kept out of school for more than 27 days', which is a different and wrong rule: the 27 days caps consecutive WORKING days, not absence. At least 20% of the child's earnings goes into a fixed deposit in a nationalised bank in the child's name, credited to them at majority.
Carry the disclaimer that all measures were taken to ensure no abuse, neglect or exploitation of the child during shooting.
Where a child and a hazard share a scene: cover it so the child is never in the hazard — doubles, separate setups, or VFX — and keep the scene clear of the guideline on children and violence.
rules.source: Child Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Amendment Rules, 2017 — rule 2C, inserted by G.S.R. 543(E) dated 2 June 2017 (draft: G.S.R. 392(E), 20 April 2017; some sites wrongly cite the draft number for the final Rules). NOTE THE TITLE: the amending notification is the CHILD LABOUR Amendment Rules; it is rule 2 of that notification which RENAMES the 1988 principal rules to 'Child and Adolescent Labour…'. The undertaking in Form C is valid six months, and the producer must also name the person responsible for the child's safety. Citation CONFIRMED 8 October 2026, including the notification number, the date and the rule number. Rule 2C covers cinema, documentary, television including reality, quiz and talent shows, radio, drama serials and anchoring. Also: the NCPCR Guidelines for Child and Adolescent Participation in the Entertainment Industry, hosted on mib.gov.in, which is the nearest thing to a primary source in this file. Plus the guidelines for certification of films as revised 16 September 2026, which bar children as victims or perpetrators of violence.
rules.uncertain: Rule 2C speaks of a 'child' (under 14). A 14-to-17-year-old is an adolescent under the Act, barred only from hazardous work; this page flags them for a person to check, not as needing the District Magistrate's permission. AND THE RULES ARE AMENDED STATE BY STATE, which matters more to this app's users than the central text does: Maharashtra amended its Child and Adolescent Labour rules in 2025 and Goa in 2024, so the central rule 2C is a floor and the applicable conditions are the ones the STATE has made. A producer shooting in Tamil Nadu should read the Tamil Nadu rules before relying on the figures above; we have not read them.
